title: Variables
description: How to store a value under a name so your program can use it again later.

content.text: The label is the variable's name. The value sits inside. Write the name later and Java hands you back what is in the box.

parts.label: type
parts.note: The kind of value the box holds. `int` means a whole number. The type always comes first.

parts.label: name
parts.note: The label you choose. You use it later to get the value back.

parts.label: assign
parts.note: Puts the value on the right into the box named on the left.

parts.label: end
parts.note: Every Java statement ends with a semicolon.

content.title: Anatomy of a variable
content.caption: Read it left to right: make a box for a whole number, call it `score`, put 100 in it.
No quotes means the value in the box. Quotes mean the exact characters you typed.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: The quotes make `"score"` plain text, so Java prints the word itself. Without quotes it would open the box and print 100.

items.sub: The type is written here, once.
After declaring, use the name alone.

items.text: Or do both on one line: `int coins = 0;`
You cannot declare the same name twice.
items.sub: A second `int lives = 3;` is an error.

content.title: What Java is holding now
content.caption: Two `int` boxes. Java already knows their type, so later lines just use the names.

content.value: A variable can get a new value as often as you like. The new value **replaces** the old one. The label stays, the contents change.

steps.note: Declare an `int` box named `lives` and put 3 in it.
Open the box and print what is inside.
Put 2 in the box. The 3 is gone. No type this time: the box already exists.
Print again. Same name, new value.
Right side first: `lives - 1` is 1. Then store that 1 back in `lives`.

content.title: Watch the box change
content.outro: `=` is not the equals of maths. It means: work this out, then store it here. Module 3 shows a shorthand, `lives--`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Java works out `x + 3` first, which is 8, then stores 8 back in `x`.

items.title: Valid
items.text: Letters, digits, `_` and `$`. Start with a letter.

items.title: Error
items.text: Cannot start with a digit. No spaces.

items: Java is case sensitive: `score` and `Score` are two different boxes.
Use **camelCase**: first word lower case, each later word starts with a capital.
Pick names that say what they mean: `daysLeft`, not `d`.
content.title: Good habits

content.question: Which one is a valid Java variable name?
content.explain: `livesLeft` uses only letters. The others start with a digit, contain a space, or use a dash.

practice.question: Declare an `int` called `age`, store your age in it, and print it with a label, like: Age: 12
Declare `int coins = 10;`, print it, then add 5 to it using `coins = coins + 5;` and print it again.
Fix the two naming mistakes in this program so it compiles.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of `int score = 100;`?
options: A type, a name, and a value.
A class, a method, and an instruction.
quiz.explain: `int` is the type (what kind of value), `score` is the name, and `100` is the value being stored.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println(score);` print when `score` holds 100?
quiz.explain: Without quotes, Java looks up what is stored under that name. With quotes it would print the word score instead.

quiz.question: Which of these is a legal Java variable name?
quiz.explain: Names cannot contain spaces or start with a digit. `highScore` also follows the camelCase style Java programmers use.

quiz.question: What does `lives = lives - 1;` do when `lives` holds 3?
options: Nothing: it is not a true statement.
quiz.explain: The right hand side is worked out first, giving 2, and that answer is then stored back under the same name.

quiz.question: Are `score` and `Score` the same variable?
options: No: Java is case sensitive, so they are two different variables.
quiz.explain: Java treats upper and lower case as different characters, so `score` and `Score` name two separate boxes.
